maths_aqa_f.1.9.summary: The gradient of a linear function tells you how steep the line is and whether it rises or falls, while the intercepts show where the line meets the axes. Interpreting these both graphically and algebraically lets you move between equations and pictures, a skill that underpins all later work in algebra and coordinate geometry. Mastery of gradients and intercepts means you can quickly sketch lines, solve real‑world problems and check your answers against the graph.

core.p: The gradient (or slope) of a straight line measures the rate of change of the dependent variable (y) with respect to the independent variable (x). It is the constant ratio of the change in y to the change in x between any two points on the line.
bullets: Calculated as **rise/run** = \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\)
Positive gradient → line rises from left to right
Negative gradient → line falls from left to right
Zero gradient → horizontal line (y‑constant)
Undefined gradient → vertical line (x‑constant, not a function in A‑level spec but noted for context)

callouts.p: The constant ratio of the change in y to the change in x for any two points on a straight line.
Gradient = (y₂‑y₁)/(x₂‑x₁)

fig.cap: A line with points (2,3) and (5,9) – gradient = (9‑3)/(5‑2)=2
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/> <line x1="50" y1="190" x2="350" y2="30" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/> <circle cx="120" cy="150" r="5" fill="#bbf7d0"/> <circle cx="280" cy="70" r="5" fill="#bbf7d0"/> <text x="115" y="165" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">(2,3)</text> <text x="275" y="85" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">(5,9)</text> <text x="200" y="120" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">gradient = 2</text></svg>

core.p: When the equation of a line is given in the form \(y = mx + c\), the coefficient \(m\) is the gradient. If the line is given in any other form, rearrange to isolate \(y\).
bullets: From \(y = mx + c\) → gradient = \(m\)
From \(ax + by = d\) → rewrite as \(y = -\frac{a}{b}x + \frac{d}{b}\); gradient = \(-a/b\)
From two points \((x₁,y₁)\) and \((x₂,y₂)\) → gradient = \((y₂-y₁)/(x₂-x₁)\)

callouts.p: Always check that you have isolated y before reading off the gradient.

core.p: The y‑intercept is the point where the line crosses the y‑axis (x = 0). In the equation \(y = mx + c\) the constant \(c\) is the y‑intercept.
bullets: Coordinate of the y‑intercept is \((0, c)\)
If \(c > 0\) the line meets the y‑axis above the origin
If \(c < 0\) it meets below the origin
If \(c = 0\) the line passes through the origin

callouts.p: The point where a straight line meets the y‑axis; its y‑coordinate is the constant term in \(y = mx + c\).

fig.cap: Line y = 2x – 3 crosses the y‑axis at (0, –3)
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/> <line x1="50" y1="190" x2="350" y2="70" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/> <circle cx="200" cy="130" r="5" fill="#fde68a"/> <text x="195" y="145" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">(0,-3)</text> <text x="200" y="120" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">y‑intercept = –3</text></svg>

core.p: The x‑intercept is where the line meets the x‑axis (y = 0). Set \(y = 0\) in the equation and solve for \(x\).
bullets: From \(y = mx + c\) → set 0 = mx + c → \(x = -c/m\)
Coordinate of the x‑intercept is \((-c/m, 0)\)
If \(c = 0\) the line passes through the origin, giving a single intercept at (0,0)

callouts.p: The point where a straight line meets the x‑axis; found by solving the equation for x when y = 0.
Do not confuse the x‑intercept with the gradient; they are different concepts.

fig.cap: For y = -½x + 4, x‑intercept is (8,0)
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/> <line x1="50" y1="190" x2="350" y2="110" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/> <circle cx="310" cy="190" r="5" fill="#bbf7d0"/> <text x="305" y="205" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">(8,0)</text> <text x="200" y="150" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">x‑intercept = 8</text></svg>

core.p: On a graph, the gradient is visualised as the steepness of the line. It can be read off by counting squares (rise over run) or by using the formula with two points.
bullets: Count vertical squares (rise) and horizontal squares (run)
If each square represents the same unit, gradient = rise/run
Steeper line → larger |gradient|
Horizontal line → gradient 0; vertical line → undefined

callouts.p: When using the grid, be consistent with the scale on both axes.

fig.cap: Grid method: rise = 4 squares, run = 2 squares → gradient = 2
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/> <line x1="100" y1="180" x2="300" y2="80" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/> <line x1="100" y1="180" x2="100" y2="80" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/> <line x1="100" y1="180" x2="200" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/> <text x="150" y="170" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">run = 2</text> <text x="120" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" transform="rotate(-90 120,130)">rise = 4</text> <text x="200" y="130" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">gradient = 2</text></svg>

core.p: From the equation you can read the intercepts directly: \(c\) gives the y‑intercept, and \(-c/m\) gives the x‑intercept (provided \(m \neq 0\)).
bullets: y‑intercept = \(c\) from \(y = mx + c\)
x‑intercept = \(-c/m\) (solve 0 = mx + c)
If \(c = 0\) both intercepts are at the origin
If \(m = 0\) the line is horizontal; no x‑intercept unless \(c = 0\)

callouts.p: x‑intercept exists only when gradient ≠ 0.

core.h: Linking gradient and intercepts to real‑world contexts
core.p: In a distance‑time graph, gradient = speed, y‑intercept = starting distance. In a cost‑quantity graph, gradient = cost per unit, y‑intercept = fixed charge.
bullets: Speed = gradient of distance‑time line
Fixed charge = y‑intercept of cost‑quantity line
Break‑even point = x‑intercept where profit becomes zero

callouts.p: State the meaning of each parameter before substituting numbers.

fig.cap: Distance‑time graph: gradient 5 m s⁻¹, y‑intercept 2 m
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/> <line x1="50" y1="190" x2="350" y2="90" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/> <text x="45" y="190" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">0</text> <text x="350" y="200" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">time</text> <text x="30" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">distance</text> <text x="200" y="130" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">gradient = 5, y‑int = 2</text></svg>

core.p: Understanding where students lose marks helps you check your work.
bullets: Mixing up the sign of the x‑intercept (using c/m instead of -c/m)
Reading the gradient from a non‑linear graph
Treating a vertical line as having a gradient of 0
Forgetting to set y = 0 when finding the x‑intercept
Confusing the constant term c with the gradient m

core.p: The mark scheme awards points for correctly stating definitions, showing work, and interpreting the result in context.
bullets: State the definition of gradient and intercepts (1 mark each).
Show algebraic rearrangement step‑by‑step (1‑2 marks).
Label the graph clearly and read off values accurately (1‑2 marks).
Interpret the meaning of the numbers in the given context (1‑2 marks).

callouts.p: Write the equation in y = mx + c form first – it saves time.

analogy.p: Imagine a road climbing a hill. The gradient tells you how many metres you rise for each metre you travel forward – just like the slope of a line. The y‑intercept is the height of the road at the foot of the hill (where you start), and the x‑intercept is the point on the ground where the road would meet the flat ground if you extended it backwards. The analogy breaks down when the road is vertical (a cliff) – then the gradient is undefined, which a straight‑line graph cannot represent in the function form y = mx + c.

terms.d: The constant ratio of change in y to change in x for a straight line; symbolised by m.
The point where a line crosses the y‑axis; its coordinate is (0,c) in y = mx + c.
The point where a line crosses the x‑axis; found by setting y = 0 and solving for x, giving (-c/m,0).
Another word for gradient; indicates steepness and direction of a line.
The vertical change between two points on a line.
The horizontal change between two points on a line.
An expression of the form y = mx + c where m is the gradient and c the y‑intercept.
The form ax + by = c; can be rearranged to y = mx + c.
A line with gradient 0; equation y = c.
A line with undefined gradient; equation x = k (not a function of y).
A point where a graph meets an axis; can be x‑ or y‑intercept.
A function whose graph is a straight line; can be written as y = mx + c.
The part of the equation that does not involve the variable x; in y = mx + c it is c.

mistakes.w: The x‑intercept is c/m
mistakes.r: The x‑intercept is -c/m; you must set y=0 and solve for x.

mistakes.w: A line with gradient 0 is vertical
mistakes.r: A gradient of 0 gives a horizontal line; a vertical line has undefined gradient.

mistakes.w: The gradient is the same as the y‑intercept
mistakes.r: Gradient (m) is the slope; y‑intercept (c) is the constant term – they are different.

mistakes.w: You can find the gradient of a curve by using rise/run
mistakes.r: Rise/run only applies to straight lines; curves have varying gradients.

mistakes.w: If c = 0 the line has no intercepts
mistakes.r: If c = 0 the line passes through the origin, giving both x‑ and y‑intercepts at (0,0).

mistakes.w: The gradient is always positive
mistakes.r: Gradient can be positive, negative, zero, or undefined depending on the line’s direction.

mistakes.w: To find the y‑intercept set x = 0 and solve for y
mistakes.r: Correct, but many students forget to state the resulting coordinate (0,c).

mistakes.w: The intercepts are the same as the roots of the equation
mistakes.r: Roots are x‑values where y = 0 (x‑intercepts); y‑intercepts are where x = 0.

exam.q: Given the line y = -3x + 6, state the gradient and the y‑intercept. (2 marks)
model: Gradient = -3 (read directly from the coefficient of x)
exam.tip: Write the equation in y = mx + c form first – it already is.

exam.q: Find the x‑intercept of the line 2y - 4x = 8. (2 marks)
exam.tip: Isolate y before substituting y = 0.

exam.q: The graph of a line passes through (1,2) and (4,8). Calculate its gradient and write the equation in y = mx + c form. (4 marks)
model: Use y = mx + c → 2 = 2·1 + c → c = 0
exam.tip: Use the two‑point formula for gradient, then substitute one point to find c.

exam.q: A car travels at a constant speed. Its distance‑time graph is a straight line passing through (0,5) and (3,20). State the speed and the distance covered at t = 5 s. (4 marks)
exam.tip: Interpret gradient as speed; then use the equation to find the required distance.

exam.q: The line y = mx + c passes through the points (0, -4) and (2, 0). Find m and c and state the meaning of each in the context of a cost‑quantity graph where y is cost (£) and x is quantity (units). (6 marks)
model: Interpretation: m = £2 per unit (variable cost), c = -£4 (fixed discount or rebate)
exam.tip: Use the intercept point to read c directly, then calculate m.

exam.q: Sketch the line with gradient -1/2 and y‑intercept 3. Label the intercepts. (4 marks)
model: From there, run 2 units right, fall 1 unit (since gradient = -1/2)
Mark another point, draw the line
exam.tip: Use the rise/run method to locate a second point before drawing.

exam.q: Explain why the line y = 4 has no x‑intercept but has a y‑intercept. (2 marks)

maths_aqa_f.1.0.summary: Algebraic notation is the universal symbolic language used across mathematics to express calculations, patterns, and relationships concisely. On AQA GCSE Foundation papers, you must fluently read, write, and interpret standard conventions including omitted multiplication signs, index notation, division as fractions, and grouping with brackets. Mastering these rules prevents catastrophic arithmetic misunderstandings and ensures you can translate worded problems into mathematically exact algebraic statements.

core.h: The Core Principles of Algebraic Notation
core.p: Algebra uses letters (variables) to represent numbers whose values are either unknown or free to vary. To keep written mathematics clean, unambiguous, and quick to write, mathematicians adopt strict formatting rules. The most fundamental rule is that operation symbols like × and ÷ are usually omitted or replaced by compact representations.
bullets: **Variables** are single letters (such as x, y, n, t) representing numerical values.
Letters written next to each other indicate **multiplication**, meaning ab is shorthand for a × b.
Numbers are always written **before** letters in a multiplicative product: write 4x, never x4.
The multiplication symbol (×) is deliberately avoided to prevent confusion with the letter x.
A single letter alone has an implicit **coefficient of 1**: x means 1x, and -y means -1y.

callouts.p: An internationally agreed standard for writing mathematical expressions clearly without redundant operation signs.

core.h: Multiplication: Writing ab in Place of a × b
core.p: Whenever two or more distinct variables are multiplied together, their letters are written directly side by side with no operational sign in between. By convention, variables within a single term are written in alphabetical order, though mathematically the order does not change the product's value.
bullets: **ab** represents exactly the same calculation as **a × b**.
For three variables, **p × q × r** is written simply as **pqr**.
Writing variables in alphabetical order (e.g. **2xy** rather than **2yx**) makes it far easier to identify like terms later.
Multiplication is **commutative**, meaning a × b = b × a, so ab = ba, but standard alphabetical order is preferred.
Never insert a dot or cross in final algebraic answers unless specifically requested in working steps.

head: Arithmetic Form
Standard Algebraic Form
Explanation
rows: Number placed in front as coefficient
Single leading coefficient followed by letters

callouts.t: Do Not Confuse Place Value with Algebra
callouts.p: In arithmetic, '35' means 3 tens and 5 units (30 + 5). In algebra, 'ab' means a × b. If a = 3 and b = 5, ab is 3 × 5 = 15, NOT 35.

core.h: Repeated Addition and Coefficients: 3y in Place of y + y + y
core.p: Just as in primary school arithmetic where 5 + 5 + 5 is simplified to 3 × 5, repeated addition of the exact same algebraic quantity is expressed as a product using a numerical coefficient placed directly in front of the letter.
bullets: **y + y + y = 3y**, which means 3 multiplied by y.
The number multiplying the variable is called the **coefficient**.
In the term **7m**, the coefficient is 7 and the variable is m.
If a variable appears without a number, such as **w**, its coefficient is **1** (since 1 × w = w).
If a negative term appears alone, such as **-k**, its coefficient is **-1**.
Distinguish clearly between repeated addition (producing a coefficient: x + x = 2x) and repeated multiplication (producing a power: x × x = x²).

callouts.p: The coefficient tells you how many copies of that variable are added together. 4y means y + y + y + y.

core.h: Powers and Index Notation: a², a³, and a²b
core.p: When a variable is multiplied by itself repeatedly, standard algebraic notation requires index notation (powers) instead of repeated letters. The base is the variable being multiplied, and the exponent (superscript) indicates how many times that base occurs as a factor.
bullets: **a²** is read as 'a squared' and represents **a × a**.
**a³** is read as 'a cubed' and represents **a × a × a**.
**a⁴** represents **a × a × a × a**, and so forth for higher integer powers.
When powers combine with other variables, such as **a²b**, this means **(a × a) × b**.

The power belongs **only** to the letter immediately to its left unless brackets are used: in **3x²**, only the x is squared (3 × x × x), whereas in **(3x)²**, both 3 and x are squared (3x × 3x = 9x²).

callouts.p: Remember: Big number in front = multiplied quantity (repeated addition). Small superscript number = power (repeated multiplication).

core.h: Division: Writing a/b in Place of a ÷ b
core.p: In GCSE algebra, the division symbol (÷) is almost never used in final answers. Division is universally written in fractional form with a horizontal fraction bar (a vinculum).
bullets: **a ÷ b** is written as **a/b** or as a vertical fraction with a on top and b on the bottom.
The fraction bar acts as an automatic grouping symbol: everything in the numerator is divided by everything in the denominator.
For example, **(x + 4) ÷ 2** is written as **(x + 4)/2**.
Writing division as a fraction clarifies order of operations without requiring extra pairs of brackets.
Never leave a division sign '÷' in an algebraic expression when asked to simplify or write in standard form.

callouts.p: The horizontal line in a fraction groups terms together. (a + b)/c means the entire sum (a + b) is divided by c.

core.h: Coefficients Written as Fractions Rather Than Decimals
core.p: AQA examiners strictly reward writing fractional coefficients rather than recurring or terminating decimals. Fractions preserve complete numerical exactness and allow seamless algebraic simplification.
bullets: Write **(1/2)x** or **x/2**, never **0.5x** in pure algebraic contexts.
For recurring decimals, fractional coefficients are essential: writing **0.33x** instead of **(1/3)x** loses accuracy and marks.
Both forms **(3/5)k** and **(3k)/5** are mathematically equivalent and fully accepted by AQA mark schemes.

callouts.p: Keep coefficients as simplified fractions. If a calculation yields 2 ÷ 3 times x, write (2/3)x or 2x/3, never 0.67x.

core.p: Brackets indicate priority in calculations and group terms together. In algebraic notation, when a number or variable is placed immediately outside a bracket without an intervening sign, multiplication is implied.
bullets: **3(x + 4)** means **3 × (x + 4)**: the entire quantity inside the bracket is multiplied by 3.
**a(b + c)** means **a × (b + c)** = ab + ac.
Brackets ensure that addition or subtraction takes place before multiplication when following BIDMAS.
In expressions like **-(x - 5)**, the minus sign outside acts as **-1 × (x - 5)**.
Failure to use brackets when translating worded phrases can completely alter the mathematical meaning: 'add 3 then double' is **2(n + 3)**, not **2n + 3**.

callouts.p: Brackets group separate terms into a single collective factor that must be evaluated or multiplied as an entire unit.

core.h: Order of Operations: Applying BIDMAS in Algebra
core.p: Algebraic notation relies upon the standard mathematical order of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction. Knowing BIDMAS allows you to decode exactly what an expression instructs you to do.
bullets: In **5 + 2x**, the multiplication **2x** occurs before the addition of 5.
In **4x²**, the index applies only to x: work out **x²** first, then multiply by 4.
In **(4x)²**, the bracket takes priority: multiply 4 by x first, then square the result (giving 16x²).
In **(x + 6)/2**, the grouping of the fraction bar means you add 6 first, then divide by 2.
In **x + 6/2**, division takes priority over addition: this simplifies to x + 3.

callouts.p: Writing 5 + 3 × n as 8n is completely wrong. Multiplication 3n comes first, so the expression is 5 + 3n, which cannot be simplified further.

core.h: Translating Worded Descriptions into Algebraic Notation
core.p: A crucial exam skill is translating plain English instructions directly into correct, fully simplified algebraic notation without superfluous symbols.
bullets: 'Multiply n by 6': write **6n** (never n × 6 or n6).
'3 more than x': write **x + 3**.
'5 less than y': write **y - 5** (not 5 - y; order matters in subtraction!).
'Half of p': write **p/2** or **(1/2)p**.
'Square t and subtract 7': write **t² - 7**.
'Subtract 7 from t, then square the result': write **(t - 7)²**.
'The sum of a and b, divided by 4': write **(a + b)/4**.

head: Worded Instruction
Correct Algebraic Notation
Incorrect Attempt
rows: Divide the product of a and b by 3

callouts.p: '4 less than n' means you start with n and reduce it by 4, giving n - 4. It does NOT mean 4 - n.

core.p: On Foundation papers, AQA frequently presents 2D shapes with side lengths labelled as algebraic expressions, asking for perimeters, areas, or expressions for specific dimensions.
bullets: **Perimeter of a rectangle** with sides of length a and b: P = a + b + a + b = **2a + 2b** or **2(a + b)**.
**Area of a rectangle** with length l and width w: Area = l × w = **lw**.
**Perimeter of an equilateral triangle** with side length s: P = s + s + s = **3s**.
**Area of a square** with side length x: Area = x × x = **x²** (not 4x; 4x is its perimeter!).
Compound lengths formed by placing rods of length x end-to-end: three rods of length x joined together form a total length of **3x**.

callouts.p: Perimeter adds dimensions (giving terms like 2x + 2y or 4s). Area multiplies dimensions (giving terms like xy or s²).

analogy.p: Algebraic notation functions exactly like sheet music. Instead of writing long-winded text like 'play a middle C note softly for one beat then double its volume', musical notation uses concise symbols, clefs, and note heads. In algebra, instead of writing 'take a secret number, multiply it by itself, multiply that by three, and add half of another number', we write 3x² + y/2. The analogy breaks down because musical notes represent sound frequencies that unfold through physical time, whereas algebraic symbols represent static mathematical quantities that obey strict logical identities regardless of time.

terms.d: A letter used to represent an unspecified numerical value or a value that can vary.
A fixed numerical value that does not change (e.g. 5, -2, 1/4).
The numerical multiplier placed directly before a variable (e.g. in 6y, the coefficient of y is 6).
A single number, a single variable, or numbers and variables multiplied together, separated by + or - signs.
One or more algebraic terms joined by operations (+, -, ×, /) without an equals sign or inequality symbol.
The result of multiplying two or more quantities together; written algebraically as ab or 4xy.
The small superscript number that indicates how many times a base is multiplied by itself (e.g. in x³, 3 is the index).
A number or variable raised to the power 2 (multiplied by itself: a² = a × a).
A number or variable raised to the power 3 (multiplied by itself twice: a³ = a × a × a).
The horizontal line separating numerator and denominator in a fraction, functioning as an implied bracket.
A coefficient written as a common fraction rather than a decimal (e.g. (3/4)x instead of 0.75x).
Using brackets or a fraction bar to specify that an operation must apply to multiple terms simultaneously.
A property where order does not affect the outcome: a × b = b × a and a + b = b + a.
A multiplication that is understood without being explicitly written, such as between 4 and x in 4x, or between 3 and (x + 2).

mistakes.w: x × x = 2x
mistakes.r: x × x = x². 2x means x + x (repeated addition). An index indicates repeated multiplication.

mistakes.w: a ÷ b = a ÷ b (leaving the division sign in an answer)
mistakes.r: Write division as a fraction: a/b with a horizontal fraction bar.
Write the numerical coefficient in front of the letter: 3y.

mistakes.w: p × p × p = 3p
mistakes.r: p × p × p = p³. 3p means p + p + p.

mistakes.w: 0.5x when asked for standard fractional form
mistakes.r: Write (1/2)x or x/2. Standard algebraic convention prefers fraction coefficients.

mistakes.w: Subtract 4 from x written as 4 - x
mistakes.r: x - 4. 'Subtract 4 from x' means you start with x and remove 4.

mistakes.w: 3(x + 2) interpreted as 3x + 2
mistakes.r: The bracket applies the multiplier 3 to every term inside: 3(x + 2) = 3 × x + 3 × 2 = 3x + 6.

mistakes.w: 2x² interpreted as (2x)² = 4x²
mistakes.r: In 2x², the power of 2 applies ONLY to x. It means 2 × x × x.

exam.q: Write down an algebraic expression for the total cost, in pence, of x apples at 30p each and y bananas at 45p each.
exam.tip: Do not write 30 × x or include a 'p' unit inside the expression itself.

exam.q: Simplify by writing in standard algebraic notation: m × m × m × m
model: m multiplied by itself 4 times is written as m⁴
exam.tip: Avoid writing 4m; that represents m + m + m + m.

exam.q:
Write each of the following in standard algebraic notation:
(a) p multiplied by q
(b) t divided by 8
(c) 5 multiplied by w multiplied by w
exam.tip: Keep terms compact: omit multiplication signs and write division as a fraction.

exam.q: Write an algebraic expression for: 'Add 7 to n, then multiply the answer by 4'.
model: Multiplying the entire result by 4 gives 4(n + 7)
exam.tip: Brackets are essential here. Writing 4n + 7 would score 0 or 1 because that doubles only n before adding 7.

exam.q:
A rectangle has width w cm. Its length is 3 cm longer than its width.
(a) Write an expression in terms of w for the length of the rectangle.
(b) Write an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle. Simplify your answer.
exam.tip: Collect all like terms together to give a fully simplified final expression.

exam.q:
State whether each statement is True or False:
(a) 2a + 3b is the same as 5ab
(b) k × k = k²
(c) y/4 is the same as 0.25y
(d) 4x² means (4x)²
model: (a) False (unlike terms cannot be combined by addition into a product)
(b) True (multiplying a letter by itself gives a power of 2)
(c) True (dividing by 4 is equivalent to multiplying by 1/4 or 0.25)
(d) False (in 4x² only x is squared; in (4x)² both 4 and x are squared to give 16x²)
exam.tip: Notice how powers bind more tightly than coefficients.

exam.q: Express the following with a fractional coefficient in simplest form: 6x ÷ 8
model: Simplify the numerical fraction 6/8 by dividing numerator and denominator by 2 to get (3/4)x or 3x/4
exam.tip: Always reduce numerical fractions to simplest terms.

exam.q:
Match each worded phrase to its correct algebraic expression.
Phrases:
(i) 5 more than double x
(ii) Double the sum of x and 5
(iii) The square of the sum of x and 5
(iv) 5 more than the square of x
Expressions: A: (x + 5)², B: 2(x + 5), C: x² + 5, D: 2x + 5
exam.tip: Trace the exact order: 'sum of x and 5' means (x + 5) must be formed inside brackets before squaring or doubling.

exam.q: Write down an expression for the area of a square whose sides each have length 3k.
model: Multiply coefficients and variables: 3 × 3 × k × k = 9k²
exam.tip: A very common error is 3k²; both the 3 and the k must be squared.

worked.q: A taxi company charges a fixed booking fee of £3.50 plus £1.75 for every mile travelled, m. Write down an algebraic expression for the total taxi fare in pounds.
steps: Identify the variable: m represents the number of miles travelled.
Identify the variable cost: £1.75 per mile means 1.75 × m = 1.75m.
Identify the constant cost: a fixed booking fee of £3.50.
Combine the two parts into a single expression by addition: 3.50 + 1.75m (or 1.75m + 3.5).

worked.q: Write down an expression for the perimeter and area of a rectangle with length (2x + 1) cm and width 4 cm.
steps: To find the perimeter, add all four sides: P = (2x + 1) + 4 + (2x + 1) + 4.
Group like terms: (2x + 2x) + (1 + 4 + 1 + 4) = 4x + 10 cm.
To find the area, multiply width by length: Area = 4 × (2x + 1).
Expand or write in bracket notation: 4(2x + 1) or 8x + 4 cm².

worked.q: Rewrite the arithmetic expression (n × n × 6) + (n ÷ 5) using standard algebraic notation.
steps: Examine the first part: n × n × 6. Repeated multiplication n × n gives n². The number 6 is the coefficient, placed at the front: 6n².
Examine the second part: n ÷ 5. Replace the division symbol with a horizontal fraction line: n/5 (or (1/5)n).
Join both parts with the addition sign: 6n² + n/5.

maths_aqa_f.1.2.summary: Specification point A3 forms the absolute grammatical foundation of GCSE algebra on the AQA specification. It requires students to clearly distinguish between terms, factors, expressions, equations, formulae, identities, and inequalities based on their formal mathematical definitions and structural properties. Mastery of this point ensures you can instantly categorise any algebraic statement on Papers 1, 2, and 3, avoiding classic mark-losing errors such as confusing a formula with an identity or an expression with an equation.

core.h: The Structural Anatomy of Algebra: Terms and Factors
core.p: Every algebraic construction is built from basic structural blocks called terms and factors. Understanding the exact boundary between terms and factors prevents fundamental classification mistakes.
bullets: A **term** is a single number, a single variable, or numbers and variables multiplied or divided together.
Terms in an algebraic statement are separated strictly by addition (+) and subtraction (-) signs.
In the expression 4x² - 7x + 5, there are three terms: +4x², -7x, and +5.
The sign (+ or -) belongs permanently to the term that immediately follows it.
A **factor** is an expression, number, or letter that divides exactly into another term or expression without leaving a remainder.
In the single term 12xy, the factors include 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, x, y, 2x, 3y, 4xy, etc.
When an expression is written in bracketed form such as 3(2x + 1), the number 3 and the bracket (2x + 1) are both factors of the whole expression.

callouts.p: A term is a single number, variable, or product/quotient of numbers and variables, separated from other terms by addition or subtraction signs.
A factor is a number, variable, or bracketed sub-expression that multiplies with another to produce a given product.

core.h: Expressions: Collections of Terms Without an Equals Sign
core.p: An expression represents an unknown numerical value or a set of mathematical operations. It contains no verb (no equals sign, identity symbol, or inequality sign).
bullets: An **expression** contains one or more terms combined with operations (+, -, ×, ÷).
An expression **never** contains an equals sign (=), an identity symbol (≡), or an inequality symbol (<, >, ≤, ≥).
Because an expression has no equals sign, it cannot be 'solved'; it can only be **simplified**, **expanded**, **factorised**, or **evaluated** by substitution.
Examples of expressions include: 3x + 2, 5a² - 2b, (x + 3)(x - 4), and 7.
A single number or single letter on its own (such as y or 14) is also formally classified as an algebraic expression containing one term.

callouts.p: Never write '= 0' at the end of an expression when simplifying or factorising. Adding an equals sign converts an expression into an equation, which forfeits the final accuracy mark in AQA mark schemes.

core.h: Equations: Stating Equality for Specific Unknown Values
core.p: An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal in value for only specific, particular values of the unknown variable.
bullets: An **equation** contains an equals sign (=) connecting two expressions.
Crucially, an equation is **only true for certain specific values** of the variable (its roots or solutions).
For example, 2x + 5 = 13 is an equation because it is only true when x = 4. If x has any other value, the statement is false.
A quadratic equation such as x² - 5x + 6 = 0 is true for exactly two values: x = 2 and x = 3.
Equations can be solved systematically by balancing operations on both sides to determine the unknown value(s).

callouts.p: If a mathematical statement with an equals sign is only true for particular numbers, it is an equation, NOT an identity and NOT a formula.

core.h: Formulae: Connecting Distinct Physical or Mathematical Variables
core.p: A formula (plural: formulae) defines a general mathematical relationship or rule connecting two or more distinct variables, typically representing real-world quantities.
bullets: A **formula** contains an equals sign (=) and **at least two different variables** (represented by different letters).
One variable is typically isolated on one side as the **subject** of the formula.
Unlike an equation in one unknown, a formula does not have a single fixed numerical solution; instead, the value of the subject changes whenever the other variables change.
Classic real-world formulae include: A = lw (Area of rectangle), C = 2πr (Circumference of circle), v = u + at (Velocity), and P = 2l + 2w (Perimeter).
If an expression containing two variables equals a third variable (e.g. S = n/2(2a + (n-1)d)), it is a formula.

callouts.t: How to Spot a Formula on AQA Papers
callouts.p: Count the letters! If there is an equals sign and two or more different letters representing quantities (like v, u, a, t or A, r), AQA categorises it as a formula.

core.h: Identities: True for Every Conceivable Value
core.p: An identity is an equation that is universally true for every possible numerical value of the variables involved.
bullets: An **identity** shows two expressions that are mathematically equivalent in all respects.
It is true for **all values** of the variable; substituting any real number into both sides will always produce a valid equality.
The formal symbol for an identity is the triple bar (≡), read as 'is identically equal to'.
AQA Foundation papers frequently use a standard equals sign (=) in identity questions, expecting students to recognise that equality holds for all values (e.g., 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).
Standard expansions and factorisations are identities: e.g. 4(3x - 5) ≡ 12x - 20, or (x + 2)(x + 3) ≡ x² + 5x + 6.
If substituting x = 0, x = 1, and x = 100 all yield true statements without altering the expressions, the statement is an identity.

callouts.p: An algebraic identity is an equality between two expressions that remains true for all conceivable numerical values of the variables.

core.p: An inequality shows that one algebraic expression or number is greater than, less than, or bounded relative to another.
bullets: An **inequality** contains an inequality symbol: < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), or ≥ (greater than or equal to).
The symbol ≠ (not equal to) also designates an inequality on Foundation papers.
Unlike equations which have distinct point solutions, inequalities usually have a continuous range or set of values as their solution.
For example, 2x + 1 > 7 solves to give x > 3, representing infinitely many real values.
Double inequalities show bounds on both sides: e.g. -2 ≤ x < 5 defines the integer values -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

core.p: AQA examiners regularly provide a table containing 4 to 6 algebraic statements and ask candidates to tick whether each is an Expression, Equation, Formula, or Identity.
bullets: Step 1: Check for a relation sign. If there is NO '=' and NO inequality symbol, it is strictly an **Expression**.
Step 2: Check for an inequality symbol (<, >, ≤, ≥, ≠). If present, it is strictly an **Inequality**.
Step 3: If it contains an '=', count the different letters. If there are two or more different variables representing connected quantities (e.g. y = 3x - 4, or A = πr²), it is a **Formula**.
Step 4: If it has an '=' and only one variable, test values. If both sides simplify to the exact same algebraic form (e.g. 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12), it is an **Identity**.
Step 5: If it has an '=' and is only true for a specific numerical value (e.g. 3x + 4 = 19), it is an **Equation**.

callouts.p: y = 2x + 1 is a formula (or equation of a line linking two variables). 2x + 1 = 9 is an equation in one variable that can be solved for x = 4.

core.p: Within algebraic expressions and equations, numbers play distinct grammatical roles depending on their position and relationship to the letters.
bullets: A **variable** is a letter that represents an unknown number or a quantity that can change in value (e.g. x, y, t).
A **coefficient** is the numerical factor multiplying a variable.
In the term 7x, the coefficient of x is 7.
In the term -x², the coefficient of x² is -1. If no number is visibly written before a variable, the coefficient is 1 or -1.
In the term x/4, the coefficient of x is 1/4 (or 0.25).
A **constant** (or constant term) is a fixed numerical value that does not change because it is not multiplied by any variable (e.g. the '+ 8' in 3x² - 2x + 8).

callouts.t: Remember the Negative Sign with Coefficients
callouts.p: In the expression 9 - 4x, the coefficient of x is -4, NOT 4. The operator belongs directly to the term that follows it.

core.p: Understanding how two expressions become an identity clarifies why expanding brackets or collecting like terms preserves algebraic truth.
bullets: Two expressions are **equivalent** if they take the same numerical value for any chosen input value of the variable.
When two equivalent expressions are set equal to each other, the resulting statement is an **identity**.
For example, the expression 2(x + 5) is equivalent to 2x + 10.
Writing 2(x + 5) ≡ 2x + 10 forms an identity.
To mathematically prove or show that an equality is an identity at Foundation level, expand or factorise one side until it matches the other side identically.

core.h: Translating Word Problems into Accurate Algebraic Forms
core.p: AQA Foundation papers frequently ask candidates to write down an expression, equation, or formula corresponding to a given real-world sentence.
bullets: If asked to write an **expression** for '5 more than 3 times a number n': write 3n + 5. (Do NOT write '= something').
If asked to write an **equation** for '5 more than 3 times a number n is 26': write 3n + 5 = 26.
If asked to write a **formula** for 'the total cost C in pounds of buying n tickets at £8 each plus a booking fee of £3': write C = 8n + 3.
If asked to write an **inequality** for 'a number n is at least 12': write n ≥ 12.
Pay obsessive attention to the wording in the prompt: providing an equation when asked for an expression results in immediate loss of marks.

callouts.t: Do Not Solve When Asked to State
callouts.p: If a question says 'Write an expression for the total age...', do not try to guess a number or solve anything. Just provide the algebraic expression in its simplest form.

analogy.p:
Think of algebra as written language: A **term** is a single vocabulary word (e.g. 'cat' or 'black_cat'). An **expression** is a descriptive phrase without a verb (e.g. 'the fast black cat'). It describes something, but does not assert a fact. An **equation** is a specific factual sentence containing a verb (e.g. 'The fast black cat is inside box number 4'). It is either true or false depending on which box you check. An **identity** is a universal truth or tautology (e.g. 'A feline is a cat'). It is always true by definition, no matter the context. A **formula** is a recipe or instruction linking independent items (e.g. 'Total_weight = cat_weight + basket_weight').

Where the analogy breaks down: In English, a phrase can stand alone conversationally, but in mathematics, expressions have exact numerical values upon substitution, and every single arithmetic operator must follow strict algebraic syntax without ambiguity.

terms.d: A single number, variable, or product/quotient of numbers and variables, separated from other terms by + or - signs.
A number, variable, or bracketed expression that divides into another expression with zero remainder, or multiplies with another to form a product.
A mathematical statement formed from terms and operation symbols (+, -, ×, ÷) that does not contain an equals, identity, or inequality sign.
A mathematical statement containing an equals sign (=) asserting that two expressions are equal for only specific values of the variable.
A general mathematical rule or relationship connecting two or more different variables, expressed with an equals sign.
An equality relationship (symbolised by ≡ or =) between two algebraic expressions that is true for all possible values of the variable(s).
A mathematical statement comparing two expressions using the symbols <, >, ≤, ≥, or ≠, showing that one value is strictly or weakly bounded by another.
The numerical multiplying factor placed directly before a variable in an algebraic term (including its positive or negative sign).
A standalone number in an algebraic expression or equation that does not contain any variables and therefore maintains a fixed value.
A letter or symbol used to represent an unknown quantity or a quantity that can take different numerical values.
The single variable that stands alone on one side of a formula with a positive coefficient of 1.
Two or more expressions that always yield the same numerical value regardless of what number is substituted into the variable.
Terms that contain the exact same variables raised to the exact same powers, differing at most by their numerical coefficients.

mistakes.w: Calling 3x + 8 = 20 an identity because it has an equals sign.
mistakes.r: 3x + 8 = 20 is an equation because it is only true for the single specific value x = 4. An identity must be true for all values of x.

mistakes.w: Classifying A = lw as an equation because it contains an equals sign.
mistakes.r: A = lw is a formula because it connects three distinct variables (A, l, and w) representing real-world measurable quantities.

mistakes.w: Adding '= 0' when asked to write an expression for 'twice a number plus 7'.
mistakes.r: Writing 2n + 7 = 0 turns an expression into an equation. The correct answer is simply 2n + 7.

mistakes.w: Stating that the coefficient of x in the expression 5 - x is 1.
mistakes.r: The sign belongs to the term that follows it. In 5 - x, the term is -x, so the coefficient is -1.

mistakes.w: Identifying 4(x + 2) = 4x + 8 as an equation.
mistakes.r: 4(x + 2) = 4x + 8 is an identity because expanding the left side gives the right side identically; it is true for any value of x.

mistakes.w: Stating that the expression 3x² - 5x + 2 has 2 terms because 3x² and -5x both contain x.
mistakes.r: It has 3 terms (3x², -5x, and +2). Terms are separated by + and - signs, and x² is not a like term with x.

mistakes.w: Classifying x + 4 > 10 as an equation.
mistakes.r: It is an inequality because it contains the greater-than symbol (>) instead of an equals sign.

mistakes.w: Thinking that an identity must always use the ≡ symbol on GCSE papers.
mistakes.r: AQA GCSE papers often write identities using a standard equals sign (=), e.g. 'Circle the identity: 2x + 4 = 2(x + 2)'. Recognise it by structural equivalence.

exam.q:
Circle the word that describes 3x - 7
[Expression, Equation, Formula, Identity]
exam.tip: It has no equals sign or inequality sign, so it must be an expression.

exam.q:
Here is a list of algebraic statements:
A: y = 4x + 3
B: 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10
C: 3x - 1 = 14
D: 5x + 2y
(a) Which statement is a formula?
(b) Which statement is an identity?
exam.tip: A links two variables y and x, making it a formula. B is algebraically identical on both sides, making it an identity.

exam.q:
Look at the statement: 4a + 3b - 7
(a) How many terms are in this expression?
(b) Write down the coefficient of b.
exam.tip: Terms are separated by plus/minus signs. The coefficient of b is the number multiplying b.

exam.q:
Match each statement to its correct description.
(i) v = u + at
(ii) 3x + 4 = 19
(iii) 2x + 3x = 5x
(iv) x + 7 < 12
exam.tip: Give one mark per correct match: Formula (links variables), Equation (solvable for x=5), Identity (true for all x), Inequality (uses <).

exam.q:
Liam says: 'x² + 4 = 8 is an identity because it contains an equals sign and a variable.'
Explain why Liam is incorrect.
model: It is an equation, not an identity, because it is only true for specific values of x (x = 2 or x = -2), not for all values of x.
exam.tip: To disprove an identity claim, state clearly that it is only true for particular numbers or give a counterexample (e.g. if x = 1, 1 + 4 ≠ 8).

exam.q: Write an expression for the total cost, in pence, of x apples at 35p each and y oranges at 45p each.
exam.tip: Do not include an equals sign or 'p' in your final algebraic expression.

exam.q:
Circle the identity.
x + 5 = 12
2x + 3 = 11
4(x - 2) = 4x - 8
y = 3x - 1
exam.tip: Expand 4(x - 2) to get 4x - 8. Because both sides are identical for every value of x, it is an identity.

exam.q:
A rectangle has length (2x + 3) cm and width 5 cm.
(a) Write down an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle in terms of x. Give your answer in its simplest form.
(b) The perimeter is 36 cm. Write down an equation connecting your perimeter expression to 36.
exam.tip: Part (a) must be an expression without '='; part (b) must be an equation containing '='.

exam.q:
Tick whether each statement is an Expression, Equation, Formula, or Identity:
(a) 5x - 3 = 17
(b) C = 2πr
(c) 7x + 2
(d) 3(2x + 1) = 6x + 3
exam.tip: One mark for each completely correct classification.

exam.q:
Consider the expression: 8 - 5x + x²
(a) State the constant term.
(b) State the coefficient of x.
exam.tip: The negative sign stays with 5x. Therefore, the coefficient is -5, not 5.

worked.q:
Classify the following four mathematical statements as an Expression, Equation, Formula, Identity, or Inequality, giving a precise mathematical reason for each:
(a) 3x + 11 = 26
(b) V = lwh
(c) 5(x + 2) ≡ 5x + 10
(d) 4x - 7 > 9
steps: Step 1: Analyse statement (a) '3x + 11 = 26'. It contains an equals sign (=) and only one variable (x). It is only true when 3x = 15, so x = 5. Because it is only true for a specific numerical value, it is an Equation.

Step 2: Analyse statement (b) 'V = lwh'. It contains an equals sign (=) connecting four distinct variables: V (volume), l (length), w (width), and h (height). Because it defines a general relationship connecting different physical quantities, it is a Formula.

Step 3: Analyse statement (c) '5(x + 2) ≡ 5x + 10'. Expanding the left-hand side gives 5 × x + 5 × 2 = 5x + 10. Both sides are identical in structure for every possible real number value of x. Because it is true for all values of the variable, it is an Identity.

Step 4: Analyse statement (d) '4x - 7 > 9'. It contains the inequality symbol '>' (strictly greater than). Because it expresses an order/inequality relationship rather than equality, it is an Inequality.
worked.ans:
(a) Equation (true only for x = 5)
(b) Formula (relates multiple variables)
(c) Identity (true for all values of x)
(d) Inequality (contains the > comparison sign)

worked.q:
For the algebraic statement 12 - 7x + 4x²:
(a) State the number of terms.
(b) Write down the term containing the variable x to the power 1.
(c) State the coefficient of x.
(d) State the coefficient of x².
(e) Identify the constant term.
steps: Step 1: Count the terms separated by addition and subtraction signs. The terms are +12, -7x, and +4x². That is a total of 3 terms.
Step 2: Locate the term with x to the first power. That is -7x (including the negative sign).
Step 3: The coefficient is the multiplying number in front of x in that term, which is -7.
Step 4: The coefficient of x² is the multiplying number directly before x², which is +4.
Step 5: The constant term is the numerical term that contains no variable, which is 12.

maths_aqa_f.1.8.summary: Linear graphs represent relationships between two variables producing a constant rate of change shown as a straight line. The standard form y = mx + c directly displays the gradient m (steepness and direction) and the y-intercept (0, c) where the line crosses the vertical axis. In AQA Foundation Maths, you must be able to calculate gradients from coordinates, form linear equations, identify parallel lines with matching gradients, and recognise perpendicular lines meeting at 90 degrees.

core.h: The General Equation of a Straight Line: y = mx + c
core.p: Every non-vertical straight line can be written in the form y = mx + c. This algebraic structure links directly to the visual appearance of the line on a Cartesian grid.
bullets: **m** represents the **gradient** (the slope or rate of change of y with respect to x).
**c** represents the **y-intercept** (the value on the y-axis where the line cuts through x = 0).
The coordinate of the y-intercept is always written as **(0, c)**.
If a line passes through the origin (0, 0), then c = 0, giving the direct proportion equation **y = mx**.
If an equation is not in the form y = mx + c (for example, 2y - 6x = 8), you must rearrange it by making y the subject before reading off m and c.

callouts.p: The measure of steepness of a line calculated as the vertical change divided by the horizontal change: m = (change in y) / (change in x).
Never read m and c directly from an equation like 3y = 9x + 6. You must first divide every single term by 3 to get y = 3x + 2, so m = 3 and c = 2.

core.h: Calculating the Gradient from Two Points
core.p: The gradient measures how many units the line goes up or down for every 1 unit moved to the right. Given any two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), the gradient is found using a ratio.
bullets: Gradient formula: **m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)**.
Change in y is often called 'rise' or vertical displacement.
Change in x is often called 'run' or horizontal displacement.
A line sloping upwards from left to right has a **positive gradient** (m > 0).
A line sloping downwards from left to right has a **negative gradient** (m < 0).
Always be careful when subtracting negative coordinates: for instance, 5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8.

callouts.p: Before using the formula, explicitly write x1, y1 above the first point and x2, y2 above the second to avoid mixing up the order.

core.p: Special straight lines are either completely horizontal or completely vertical, and their equations do not follow the standard two-variable pattern in the same way.
bullets: **Horizontal lines** have the equation **y = k**, where k is a constant value. The y-coordinate is identical for all points.
The gradient of any horizontal line is **0** because change in y is 0.
The x-axis has the equation **y = 0**.
**Vertical lines** have the equation **x = k**, where k is a constant value. The x-coordinate is identical for all points.
The gradient of a vertical line is **undefined** (division by zero horizontal change).
The y-axis has the equation **x = 0**.

callouts.p: Students often swap the axis equations: the x-axis is y = 0, and the y-axis is x = 0.

core.h: Finding the Equation of a Line Given Gradient and a Point
core.p: When given the gradient m and one point (x, y) on the line, you can find the complete equation y = mx + c by determining the constant c.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the skeleton equation **y = mx + c** with the known gradient substituted for m.
Step 2: Substitute the known values of **x** and **y** from the given point into this equation.
Step 3: Solve the resulting linear equation to find the numerical value of **c**.
Step 4: Rewrite the full equation containing both the values of m and c.

callouts.p: Substitute the x-value of your point back into your final equation: the resulting y-value must match your given point exactly.

core.h: Finding the Equation of a Line Given Two Points
core.p: Finding the equation between two arbitrary points combines finding the gradient first, then solving for the y-intercept.
bullets: Step 1: Find the gradient m using **m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)**.
Step 2: Choose either of the two points (x1, y1) or (x2, y2); picking positive numbers makes calculations easier.
Step 3: Substitute m and your chosen point into **y = mx + c**.
Step 4: Solve for **c**.
Step 5: Write out the completed equation: **y = mx + c**.

core.p: Parallel lines run in exactly the same direction and never intersect, no matter how far they are extended in either direction.
bullets: Two lines are **parallel** if and only if they have the **exact same gradient**.
If Line 1 has equation y = m1*x + c1 and Line 2 has equation y = m2*x + c2, then they are parallel if **m1 = m2**.
Parallel lines have different y-intercepts (c1 != c2); if c1 = c2, they are the identical line.
Example: y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 8 are parallel because both have m = 3.
To check if two implicit equations are parallel, rearrange both into y = mx + c form and compare their x-coefficients.

callouts.p: Lines are parallel when their gradients are equal: m1 = m2.

core.p: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle (90 degrees). Their slopes have a precise mathematical relationship.
bullets: The gradient of a perpendicular line is the **negative reciprocal** of the original gradient.
If a line has gradient m, any perpendicular line has gradient **-1/m**.
The product of the gradients of two perpendicular lines is always **-1** (m1 * m2 = -1).
If m = 2, the perpendicular gradient is -1/2.
If m = -3/4, the perpendicular gradient is +4/3 (flip the fraction and change the sign).
Special case: A horizontal line (m = 0) is perpendicular to a vertical line (m undefined).

callouts.p: A number formed by inverting a fraction (swapping numerator and denominator) and reversing its positive/negative sign.

core.h: Rearranging Equations into y = mx + c Form
core.p: Exam questions often present equations in implicit forms such as ax + by = d. You must rearrange to isolate y before identifying properties.
bullets: Goal: Get y entirely alone on the left-hand side with a coefficient of +1.
Step 1: Move x-terms and constant terms not attached to y to the other side by adding or subtracting.
Step 2: Divide every single term on both sides by the coefficient in front of y.
From this, gradient m = -1.5 and y-intercept = (0, 6).

callouts.p: When dividing by the number in front of y, do not forget to divide the constant term as well as the x-term.

core.h: Determining if a Point Lies on a Line
core.p: To check whether a specific point (x, y) lies on a given line, test whether the coordinates satisfy the line's equation.
bullets: Substitute the given x-value into the equation.
Calculate the resulting y-value.
If the calculated y matches the point's y-value, the point **lies on the line**.
If the calculated y does not match, the point **does not lie on the line**.
Alternatively, substitute both x and y into the rearranged equation and check if Left Hand Side = Right Hand Side.

core.h: Summary of Line Forms and Relationships
core.p: A structured overview consolidating line equations, gradients, and geometric orientations across the specification.
bullets: General equation: y = mx + c.
Gradient between two points: m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
Parallel lines: Equal slopes (m1 = m2).
Perpendicular lines: Negative reciprocals (m1 * m2 = -1).
Horizontal lines: y = constant (slope = 0).
Vertical lines: x = constant (slope is undefined).

analogy.t: The Ski Slope and Starting Elevation
analogy.p: Imagine a straight ski slope on a mountain. The y-intercept (c) is the base altitude where your run crosses the central timing gate at marker x = 0. The gradient (m) is the steepness and direction of the slope: a positive gradient means you are climbing uphill, while a negative gradient means you are skiing downhill. A steeper slope has a larger numerical value of m. Parallel slopes are built side-by-side at the exact same incline so skiers descend at matching angles without ever crossing paths. A perpendicular cross-path cuts across the slope directly at 90 degrees. This analogy breaks down because real ski slopes have bumps and changing steepness, whereas a mathematical straight line has an identical, unchanging gradient along its entire infinite length.

terms.d: The rate of vertical change with respect to horizontal change along a straight line; calculated as (change in y) / (change in x).
The point where a line crosses the vertical y-axis, occurring at coordinate (0, c).
The point where a line crosses the horizontal x-axis, occurring where y = 0.
Two or more lines in the same plane that never meet and have identical gradients.
Two lines that intersect at a right angle (90 degrees); their gradients multiply to -1.
The value obtained by flipping a number into a fraction and negating its sign; for a value m, it is -1/m.
An algebraic equation of the first degree whose graphical plot produces a single straight line.
Points that lie along the exact same straight line.
The vertical difference between two points on a graph (y2 - y1).
The horizontal difference between two points on a graph (x2 - x1).
The central reference point (0, 0) on a Cartesian coordinate grid where the axes intersect.
How much the dependent variable changes per unit increase in the independent variable; equal to the gradient.

mistakes.w: Saying the gradient of 2y = 6x + 4 is 6.
mistakes.r: Divide every term by 2 first to get y = 3x + 2; the gradient is 3.

mistakes.w: Writing m = (x2 - x1) / (y2 - y1) when finding a gradient.
mistakes.r: Gradient is change in y over change in x: m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).

mistakes.w: Thinking the perpendicular gradient of 3 is -3.
mistakes.r: Take the negative reciprocal: the perpendicular gradient is -1/3.

mistakes.w: Stating that the line x = 4 has a gradient of 4 and y-intercept 4.
mistakes.r: x = 4 is a vertical line; its gradient is undefined and it never crosses the y-axis.

mistakes.w: Writing the equation of the x-axis as x = 0.
mistakes.r: The x-axis has the equation y = 0 because every point on it has a y-coordinate of 0.

mistakes.w: Subtracting negative coordinates incorrectly: e.g. 4 - (-2) = 2.
mistakes.r: Subtracting a negative creates an addition: 4 - (-2) = 4 + 2 = 6.

mistakes.w: Assuming parallel lines must pass through the same y-intercept.
mistakes.r: Parallel lines have the same gradient but different y-intercepts.

mistakes.w: Writing a y-intercept as just '5' when the question asks for coordinates.
mistakes.r: Coordinates require brackets and both axes values: write (0, 5).

exam.q: Write down the gradient and the coordinates of the y-intercept of the line with equation y = 5x - 3.
exam.tip: Always write the intercept as a full coordinate (0, c) if coordinates are requested.

exam.q: A straight line passes through the points (1, 3) and (5, 11). Find the gradient of this line.
exam.tip: Show the substitution step clearly before simplifying.

exam.q: Line A has equation y = 4x - 1. Line B is parallel to Line A and passes through the point (0, 7). Write down the equation of Line B.
exam.tip: Parallel means the gradient is identical (m = 4). The point (0, 7) gives c = 7 directly.

exam.q: Rearrange the equation 3x + y = 8 into the form y = mx + c. Hence, state its gradient.
exam.tip: Subtract 3x from both sides. Don't lose the minus sign in front of 3.

exam.q: Line L has equation y = 2x + 5. Write down the gradient of a line that is perpendicular to Line L.
exam.tip: Take the negative reciprocal of 2.

exam.q: Show that the lines with equations 2y = 8x + 6 and y - 4x = -5 are parallel.
model: Second line: y = 4x - 5, so m2 = 4; both gradients are 4, hence the lines are parallel
exam.tip: Both lines must be rearranged into y = mx + c and their gradients explicitly compared.

exam.q: Find the equation of the straight line that passes through the point (2, 9) with a gradient of 3. Give your answer in the form y = mx + c.
exam.tip: Substitute x = 2 and y = 9 carefully to evaluate c.

exam.q: Find the equation of the line passing through (0, -2) and (4, 6).
model: Since line passes through (0, -2), the y-intercept c = -2
exam.tip: Notice that (0, -2) is already the y-intercept, saving you substitution time.

exam.q: Does the point (3, 13) lie on the line y = 4x + 1? You must show working to justify your answer.
model: Calculated y matches the coordinate y-value, so yes, the point lies on the line
exam.tip: State a clear final conclusion: 'Yes' or 'No' with calculation shown.

exam.q: A line passes through (-1, 5) and (3, -3). (a) Find its gradient. (b) Find its full equation.
exam.tip: Check with the other point: -2(-1) + 3 = 2 + 3 = 5, which confirms accuracy.

worked.q: Find the equation of the straight line that passes through the points A(2, 1) and B(6, 9).
steps: Step 1: Calculate the gradient m using (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1). m = (9 - 1) / (6 - 2) = 8 / 4 = 2.
Step 2: Write the equation with m = 2: y = 2x + c.
Step 3: Substitute point A(2, 1) into the equation: 1 = 2(2) + c.
Step 4: Solve for c: 1 = 4 + c, so c = 1 - 4 = -3.
Step 5: Write the complete equation: y = 2x - 3.

worked.q: Line L1 has equation 4x + 2y = 10. Find: (a) the gradient of L1, (b) the equation of the line parallel to L1 passing through (1, 6), and (c) the gradient of a line perpendicular to L1.
steps: Step 1: Rearrange 4x + 2y = 10 to make y the subject: 2y = -4x + 10, then divide by 2: y = -2x + 5. The gradient of L1 is -2.
Step 2: A parallel line has the same gradient m = -2. Its equation is y = -2x + c.
Step 3: Substitute point (1, 6) into y = -2x + c: 6 = -2(1) + c => 6 = -2 + c => c = 8. Parallel line: y = -2x + 8.
Step 4: A perpendicular line has gradient -1 / m = -1 / (-2) = +1/2.

maths_aqa_f.1.7.summary: Working with coordinates in all four quadrants is a fundamental skill in GCSE Mathematics. It involves accurately reading, plotting, and manipulating ordered pairs of numbers $(x, y)$ across positive and negative Cartesian axes. Mastering this topic allows students to solve geometric problems, calculate line segment midpoints, find distances along grid lines, and determine missing vertices of 2D shapes.

core.h: The Cartesian Coordinate System and Axes
core.p: The Cartesian coordinate system uses two perpendicular number lines that cross at right angles to locate any point in a two-dimensional plane.
bullets: The horizontal line is the **$x$-axis**, running left (negative) to right (positive).
The vertical line is the **$y$-axis**, running down (negative) to up (positive).
The point where the two axes intersect is called the **origin**, which has coordinates **$(0, 0)$**.
Coordinates are always written as an **ordered pair** in brackets separated by a comma: **$(x, y)$**.

callouts.p: The fixed reference point $(0,0)$ where the $x$-axis and $y$-axis cross at right angles.
Always read or plot the $x$-coordinate first, then the $y$-coordinate. A helpful mnemonic is 'along the corridor, then up (or down) the stairs'.

core.p: The intersecting axes divide the 2D plane into four regions known as **quadrants**, numbered counter-clockwise starting from the top-right.
bullets: **1st Quadrant (Top-Right):** Both coordinates are positive $(+x, +y)$.
**2nd Quadrant (Top-Left):** $x$ is negative, $y$ is positive $(-x, +y)$.
**3rd Quadrant (Bottom-Left):** Both coordinates are negative $(-x, -y)$.
**4th Quadrant (Bottom-Right):** $x$ is positive, $y$ is negative $(+x, -y)$.

callouts.p: Looking only at the signs of $x$ and $y$ immediately tells you which quadrant a point lies in.

core.h: Points Lying Directly on the Axes
core.p: Special attention must be paid to points that sit directly on either axis. These points have one coordinate equal to zero.
bullets: Any point lying on the **$x$-axis** has a $y$-coordinate of zero: **$(x, 0)$**. Examples: $(3, 0)$, $(-4, 0)$.
Any point lying on the **$y$-axis** has an $x$-coordinate of zero: **$(0, y)$**. Examples: $(0, 5)$, $(0, -2)$.
The origin $(0, 0)$ lies on both axes simultaneously.

callouts.p: Students often confuse $(0, 4)$ with $(4, 0)$. Remember: $(0, 4)$ means move 0 units sideways and 4 units UP (on the $y$-axis). $(4, 0)$ means 4 right and 0 up (on the $x$-axis).

core.p: To find the distance between two points that lie on a line parallel to either the $x$-axis or $y$-axis, find the difference between their changing coordinates.
bullets: **Horizontal distance** (same $y$-coordinates): Subtract the smaller $x$-coordinate from the larger $x$-coordinate: $\text{Distance} = x_2 - x_1$.
**Vertical distance** (same $x$-coordinates): Subtract the smaller $y$-coordinate from the larger $y$-coordinate: $\text{Distance} = y_2 - y_1$.
When spanning across negative and positive values, remember that subtracting a negative number is equivalent to adding its positive magnitude.

callouts.p: Lengths and distances cannot be negative. For example, the distance between $x = -4$ and $x = 3$ is $3 - (-4) = 7$ units.

core.h: Finding the Midpoint of Two Coordinates
core.p: The midpoint is the point halfway along a straight line segment joining two given points.
bullets: To calculate the midpoint of $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$, find the **average of the $x$-coordinates** and the **average of the $y$-coordinates**.
Midpoint formula: $\text{Midpoint} = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right)$.
Be careful with signs when adding negative numbers.

callouts.p: Verify your midpoint by checking if the step from $x_1$ to $x_{\text{mid}}$ is equal to the step from $x_{\text{mid}}$ to $x_2$.

core.p: Grid coordinates can be used to complete geometric shapes such as squares, rectangles, parallelograms, and kites using vector movement (step counts).
bullets: **Rectangles & Squares:** Opposite sides are equal and parallel. The change in $x$ and $y$ from one vertex to another must match the opposite side.

**Parallelograms:** To find the fourth vertex $D$ from $A$, $B$, and $C$, calculate the movement vector from $A$ to $B$ (e.g., $+3$ right, $+2$ up) and apply the exact same movement to $C$ to find $D$.
Alternatively, use the property that diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other (have the exact same midpoint).

callouts.p: If side $AB$ goes right by $dx$ and up by $dy$, then side $DC$ must also go right by $dx$ and up by $dy$.

core.h: Symmetry and Reflection across Coordinate Axes
core.p: Reflecting points across the axes follows straightforward rules regarding coordinate signs.
bullets: **Reflection in the $x$-axis ($y = 0$):** The $x$-coordinate stays the same; the $y$-coordinate changes sign: $(x, y) \rightarrow (x, -y)$.
**Reflection in the $y$-axis ($x = 0$):** The $y$-coordinate stays the same; the $x$-coordinate changes sign: $(x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)$.
**Reflection in the origin $(0,0)$:** Both coordinates change sign: $(x, y) \rightarrow (-x, -y)$.

core.p: Not all examination questions use grids scaled by 1 unit per square. Reading scales accurately is essential.
bullets: Always calculate the value of **one grid square** before reading or plotting.
Determine the scale by dividing the total value difference between labelled grid lines by the number of squares between them.
Check both the horizontal ($x$) scale and vertical ($y$) scale independently, as they may be different.

callouts.p: Do not assume that 1 grid square = 1 unit. A grid might have 1 square = 2 units on the $x$-axis but 1 square = 5 units on the $y$-axis.

analogy.p: Think of the coordinate plane like a GPS sat-nav system tracking a vehicle. The origin $(0,0)$ is the main crossroad city centre. Moving East is $+x$, West is $-x$, North is $+y$, and South is $-y$. Giving your location as $( -3, 4 )$ is like telling the sat-nav you are 3 miles West and 4 miles North of the city centre. This analogy breaks down because real-world roads are not aligned to a perfect square grid, and real terrain involves 3D elevation (height) rather than a flat 2D plane.
